locations: src/CLI/Passes.jl:1158-1169 (the new build-record gate in close())
src/CLI/Passes.jl:907-916 (audit_coverage, the sibling pattern this claims to reuse)
findings.description: The new build-staleness gate in Passes.close() reuses the raw `Git.changed_paths` diffing primitive but not the reachability guard (`cat-file -e`) that makes the same primitive safe in `audit_coverage`, so an unreachable or invalid `b["head"]` is silently read as 'the build is still fresh' instead of refusing.
findings.after: close() now does: `moved = Git.changed_paths(root, "$(b["head"])..HEAD", Preflight.covered_paths(cfg)); isempty(moved) || push!(fails, "the recorded docs build is stale — ...")`. `Git.changed_paths` is `String.(filter(!isempty, split(something(run(root, "diff", "--name-only", range, "--", paths...), ""), '\n')))`, and `Git.run` catches every exception (a bad revision included) and returns `nothing`, which `changed_paths` turns into `String[]`. I confirmed empirically that `git diff <bad-ref>..HEAD` throws `ProcessFailedException` in Julia, so a `b["head"]` that is no longer a valid commit makes `moved` come back empty — the gate reads that as 'nothing changed since the build ran' and lets the round close on it.
findings.before: Before this diff nothing recorded a build's verdict at all, so close() had no staleness question to answer.
findings.why_it_matters: The docstring on this new code claims parity with an existing, hardened pattern: "The staleness test is the one `audit_after_code` uses." But `audit_after_code`'s own helper, `audit_coverage`, explicitly guards this exact failure mode — it checks `Git.run(root, "cat-file", "-e", ah * "^{commit}") !== nothing` before trusting a `changed_paths` diff against a recorded head, precisely because (its own docstring says) "an audit whose head is unreachable proves nothing either way" and treats that as NOT covering. The new build-staleness check omits that guard, so it fails open rather than closed in exactly the scenario its sibling was written to fail closed in. This is the same class of incident the whole feature exists to prevent (a round closing on a build verdict that no longer reflects the tree) — it just needs the build's own recorded head, not the round's opening head, to have gone bad, e.g. from a hand-edited ROUND.toml (which this same diff's own scripts_refreshed feature shows already happens in this project) or a rewritten local commit.
findings.title: close()'s new docs-build staleness check trusts an unreachable recorded head as 'not stale' instead of refusing
findings.evidence: `moved = Git.changed_paths(root, "$(b["head"])..HEAD", Preflight.covered_paths(cfg))` (src/CLI/Passes.jl:1167) vs. `!isempty(ah) && Git.run(root, "cat-file", "-e", ah * "^{commit}") !== nothing && isempty(Git.changed_paths(root, "$ah..HEAD", dirs))` (src/CLI/Passes.jl:914-915).

Git.changed_paths swallows a failed git invocation (`something(run(…), "")`), so an unresolvable range is indistinguishable from a clean one. The sibling four hundred lines down already models the right shape — check reachability, and refuse with a named UNCHECKABLE fail — and the comment asserts parity with it that the code does not have.

findings.description: The underlying defect — a documented `RULE.CIT.DOI` waiver being silently void because apply_ledger resolved only the catalogue's canonical `rule` column — was real and worth fixing. The edit is wider than that defect: it makes EVERY rule in the scan's `check` closure a kill switch for the whole scan, in both directions, for all three multi-rule scans. The diff's own docstring concedes the consequence ("a waiver on either rule still disables the WHOLE scan, so it withdraws enforcement of a sibling rule the consumer never exempted") and calls it a known limit, but the limit is not pre-existing: before this diff a waiver on the non-canonical rule did nothing at all, so nothing could be withdrawn by it. A narrower repair was available and is not attempted — refusing (or reporting DEAD) when a policy waiver names a rule the scan enforces but cannot attribute, which converts a silent withdrawal of enforcement into a loud one, is the direction the rest of this package takes (`apply_ledger` already throws LedgerError when a text scan meets an `arg_type` predicate it cannot evaluate). The oracle does not cover the new direction: the added testset asserts the DOI case, the canonical case, and that `RULE.DOC.NO_DEAD_REFS` waives nothing — but RULE.DOC.NO_DEAD_REFS is unrelated to SCAN.DOI_CROSSCHECK, so the assertion that an unrelated rule waives nothing says nothing about the sibling-withdrawal case, and neither SCAN.DEAD_REF nor SCAN.API_PAGE_STRUCTURE is exercised at all.
